questions.question: Define a transverse pulse and amplitude, and explain what is transferred along the rope when a pulse travels and what is not.
questions.expected_answer: A pulse is a single disturbance moving through a medium. In a transverse pulse the particles of the medium move at right angles — perpendicular — to the direction in which the pulse travels: a knot on the rope moves straight up and down while the pulse moves horizontally. The amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle of the medium from its rest (equilibrium) position, measured in metres from the rest line to the point of maximum displacement — never from trough to crest. What travels along the rope is the disturbance and the energy it carries; the medium itself is not transferred — each particle does a short round trip and returns to its rest position. A pulse is a transfer of energy without a transfer of matter.

questions.question: State the principle of superposition. A crest of displacement plus 0,3 m meets a trough of displacement minus 0,2 m. Give the resultant displacement at complete overlap, name the type of interference, and describe the pulses afterwards.
questions.expected_answer: The principle of superposition states that when two or more pulses occupy the same point at the same time, the displacement of the medium at that point is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements — the displacements are added with their signs. Here the resultant is plus 0,3 plus minus 0,2, which is plus 0,1 m: a small hump of 0,1 m. Because the pulses displace the medium in opposite directions and the resultant is smaller than the larger pulse, this is destructive interference. After the overlap both pulses pass through each other and continue completely unchanged — each keeps its original shape, amplitude and direction of travel.

questions.question: Two pulses of equal amplitude but opposite displacement meet and the rope is momentarily flat. Explain why this is not the end of the pulses, and why the speed of a pulse cannot be increased by flicking harder.
questions.expected_answer: At the instant of complete overlap the displacements sum to zero everywhere, so the rope looks flat, but both pulses still exist: the energy of the pulses is momentarily stored in the motion — the kinetic energy — of the rope's particles, which are still moving even though their displacement is zero. A moment later the crest emerges on one side and the trough on the other, both with their original amplitude and direction. Flat does not mean gone. Flicking harder only increases the energy given to the pulse, which appears as a larger amplitude. The speed of a pulse is a property of the medium — it depends on the tension in the rope and the mass of the rope — so on the same rope every pulse travels at the same speed regardless of its size; only changing the medium, for example stretching the rope tighter, changes the speed.
